name: Native American Church
info: The Native American Church, also called Peyotism and Peyote Religion, is a syncretic Native American religion that joins traditional beliefs with elements of Christianity and the sacramental use of peyote, and arose in the Oklahoma Territory in the late nineteenth century.

facts.origin: The Oklahoma Territory (1890–1907) in the late nineteenth century, after peyote was introduced to the southern Great Plains from Mexico.
facts.founder: none: it grew among Native American peoples of the southern Great Plains; figures named in its development include Chevato, Jim Aton, John Wilson, Jonathan Koshiway and Victor Griffin.
facts.scriptures: none: ceremonies draw on prayer, peyote songs and drumming; the Cross-fire way also uses Bible readings, and the Half-Moon way uses no Bible.
facts.followers: An estimated 300,000 adherents in the United States, Canada and Mexico.

t: The church is monotheistic: members believe in a supreme being, the Great Spirit or Creator, and use peyote as a sacrament that they hold to be a means of communicating with the Great Spirit.
It has two main ways, the Half-Moon way and the Cross-fire way, which differ in whether a Bible, baptism and a minister are used.
Its use of peyote came under federal drug law in 1970 and was later protected by the American Indian Religious Freedom Act of 1978 and the Religious Freedom Restoration Act of 1993.

sections.origins:
The Native American Church, also known as Peyotism and Peyote Religion, is a syncretic Native American religion that combines traditional Native American beliefs with elements of Christianity, especially some of the Ten Commandments, and the sacramental use of the entheogen peyote. It originated in the Oklahoma Territory (1890–1907) in the late nineteenth century, after peyote was introduced to the southern Great Plains from Mexico.

Many denominations of mainstream Christianity had tried to convert Native Americans in the Western Hemisphere. These efforts were partly successful, and the religious practices of many Native American tribes, those of the Native American Church included, reflect Christian creeds. Conversion to Christianity was a slow process, but the tenets of the Native American Church were more readily accepted. The church included Protestant characteristics in its formation.

The church has more than one date for its founding as an institution. Victor Griffin, known as the last chief of the Quapaw tribe, is noted for facilitating its incorporation under Oklahoma law in 1911; the original charter of the Native American Church of the United States dates from 1913; and the church was officially created in 1918. Early in the twentieth century anthropologists led by James Mooney testified before legislative bodies on behalf of Peyotists and encouraged the movement's leaders to consolidate peyote use into an established religion whose practice would be protected by law.
sections.beliefs:
The Native American Church is monotheistic, believing in a supreme being called the Great Spirit, also referred to as the Creator or God. Its tenets regard peyote as a sacred and holy sacrament and use it as a means to communicate with the Great Spirit. Members also believe in the Trinity of God, Jesus and the Holy Ghost, which in Half-Moon rituals is represented by the three leaders present.

Members believe that disease and death result from an imbalance in the individual. Besides peyote, other sacred plants, prayer and fasting are used to cure this imbalance. Peyote is never used for recreation, and its hallucinogenic effects are considered spiritual visions; to most Native Americans, visions are a communion with the metaphysical. Not every member experiences hallucinogenic effects during peyote rituals. The plant is meant to heal or fix social, personal and communal problems, and members believe it is safe for children and pregnant women.

Services are held on special request by a family, whether to celebrate a birthday, hold a memorial or funeral, cure illness, mark a school graduation or another significant life event, or keep a Christian holiday such as Easter or Christmas. A participant sits up all night, giving up a full night's rest as a small sacrifice to the Holy Spirit and Jesus.
sections.texts:
The church has no scripture of its own. Its ceremonies include scripture reading, prayer, singing and drumming, and the use of the Bible differs between its ways. In the Cross-fire way a Bible is placed on an altar and Bible sections are recited according to the family's prayer for the particular service; among the Lakota, Cross-fire groups use the Bible for sermons, which Half-Moon followers reject, although both teach a similar Christian morality.

Music is central to a service. The singer holds a gourd rattle staff and is joined by a water-drummer with a water drum; the singer sings four songs, concludes the set, and passes the staff, gourd and drum to the next relative. Only these two instruments are used in an authentic prayer service. The songs are in what is called the peyote language, which parallels words in the Coahuilteco and Comecrudo languages of South Texas. It was introduced by the Carrizo and Coahuiltecan people of South Texas, and it makes up the songs sung around all fireplaces, whatever the tribe or denomination; these are the songs people consider "straight". Many tribes also work their own language into peyote songs, which ties a song to one tribe rather than leaving it intertribal.

Among the Menominee, prayers were said in Menomini and ended with "In the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost. Amen", taken from the Trinitarian baptismal formula. N. Scott Momaday gives a portrayal of the peyote service in his novel House Made of Dawn.
sections.spread:
The church is today the most widespread indigenous religion among Native Americans in the United States (except Alaska Natives and Native Hawaiians), in Canada, among First Nations people in Saskatchewan and Alberta, and in Mexico, with an estimated 300,000 adherents.

It has several ways, or traditions. The two main ones are the Half-Moon way and the Cross-fire way. The Half-Moon way was introduced in 1914 or 1924 by James Seymour, who was a member of the Winnebago tribe. Among the Menominee, Peyotism is described as unique, with Catholic beliefs and practices incorporated after years of Catholic missionaries, though Protestantism has also had an influence. Many Cross-fire adherents, such as the Dakota Cross-fire and Winnebago Cross-fire members, strongly oppose the use of tobacco and smoking in rituals and ceremonies. Prominent figures in the church's development include Chevato, Jim Aton, John Wilson and Jonathan Koshiway, and Victor Griffin helped spread the religion to some other related tribes in the region.

The fireplaces, the ceremonial peyote altars passed down in families, vary greatly with tribe and environment, and some special fireplaces fit neither main style. The Half-Moon fireplace uses a half-moon shaped sand altar and tobacco and corn-shucks, and its staff is passed around the tipi. The Cross-Fire fireplace uses a horseshoe shaped sand altar with a mound outside the tipi to represent the "grave of Jesus Christ", no tobacco, and a staff placed upright in the ground.
sections.community:
Ceremonies are generally held in a tipi and must be conducted by a priest, pastor or elder known as the Roadman. He is assisted by a Fireman, who tends the holy fireplace so that it burns steadily all night. The Roadman may use a prayer staff, a beaded and feathered gourd, a small drum, cedar and his eagle feather. Services commonly begin at sundown on a Friday or Saturday evening and end at sunrise. Very early, between 4:30 and 5:00 in the morning, the Roadman's wife or another female relative prepares four sacramental foods: water, shredded beef or "sweet meat", corn mush and a variety of berries. A second breakfast is served well after sunrise, just before the service closes.

The service is followed by a feast for the whole community. The sponsoring family then gives gifts to the Roadman and all his helpers to show deep appreciation for their work.

In the United States there are two main umbrella chapters. The Native American Church of the United States holds the original 1913 charter, and its chapters have no blood quantum requirement to attend ceremonies. The Native American Church of North America, an offshoot from the late 1960s, admits only Native Americans with a blood quantum of one quarter or more, checked through Certificates of Degree of Indian or Alaska Native Blood and church membership cards. It is in the minority nationally. Both have tribal offshoots, notably among the Navajo.
sections.legacy:
As the United States government became more involved in controlling drugs, the church faced possible legal difficulties over peyote. The Controlled Substances Act, signed by President Richard Nixon in 1970, prohibited possession of psychedelics such as peyote and classified them as controlled drugs. The American Indian Religious Freedom Act of 1978 was passed to protect the church's use of the plant, and federal rulings such as US v. Boyll (1991) and the Religious Freedom Restoration Act of 1993 allow members to transport, possess and use peyote for religious purposes.

Such use has been declared legal without regard to race or tribal status in all states other than Idaho and Texas, which have outlawed use by non-natives. Peyote can be bought from licensed distributors in Texas, who sell wild peyote gathered by licensed collectors, only by enrolled tribal members with a permit and the intent to use it for religious purposes. The Neo-American Church tried to claim LSD and marijuana as sacraments, and the courts ruled against it. Reuben Snake, a Ho-Chunk roadman, worked towards the American Indian Religious Freedom Act.

The church also left a body of art: gourd rattles, feather fans, ritual staffs and drum sticks carved with tipis, birds, stars and sun patterns, made with European trade beads and metal as well as traditional materials, along with paintings and jewellery.

summary: The Native American Church is a syncretic Native American religion that joins traditional beliefs with elements of Christianity and the sacramental use of peyote. It arose in the Oklahoma Territory in the late nineteenth century and has an estimated 300,000 adherents in the United States, Canada and Mexico. Its legal protection for peyote came through federal laws of 1978 and 1993.
references: David F. Aberle, The Peyote Religion among the Navajo (University of Oklahoma Press, 1991)
Omer C. Stewart, Peyote Religion: A History (University of Oklahoma Press, 1987)
notes: Founding dates conflict: the article says the church originated in the Oklahoma Territory (1890–1907), incorporation under Oklahoma law in 1911 (Victor Griffin), an original charter of 1913 'in Oklahoma territory' (the territory had ended in 1907), and that it 'was officially created in 1918'. All are reported side by side; start 1890 is the opening of the Territory period, circa.
James Seymour's Half-Moon way: 1914 or 1924 in the article; the event label uses 1914 and says 'in 1914 or 1924'.

The article says the American Indian Religious Freedom Act passed 'after his death in 1994' for Reuben Snake, which contradicts the 1978 date given elsewhere; his death year is left out and the 1978 date is used.

The article also says it 'seems' the Cross-fire opposition to tobacco comes from Protestant sects rather than Jehovah's Witnesses; left out. The article's 'persecution' heading covers only legal history, so no persecution is described.

Menominee Peyotism is described as 'historically' unique; written in the past where the article does. The article's origin sentence says it is the most widespread indigenous religion among Native Americans in the US, Canada (First Nations in Saskatchewan and Alberta) and Mexico; reproduced with its exceptions.

Details of ceremony are given only as far as the article does. References left empty for the editor; the article's Further reading lists Aberle (1991), Stewart (1987), Slotkin (1952) and Hayward (2011).

Faith map: coordinates are mine for places the article names (Oklahoma, Saskatchewan and Alberta, South Texas, Mexico, Navajo country); the Navajo area starts 1913 only in the sense of the article's remark that the Navajo have major chapters in both umbrella chapters, whose dates are 1913 and late 1960s; the Mexican, Canadian and Navajo areas are dated from 1918 and are my choice of start.
